# Free Mortgage Calculator: How to Use?
Our free mortgage loan calculator helps home buyers evaluate financing scenarios across the USA, UK, Canada, and Australia. By calculating true monthly housing costs, statutory compounding rules, and customized multi-year amortization schedules, this tool provides complete transparency into borrowing costs and potential extra payment interest savings.
# Advanced Compounding & Loan Payoff Analysis
Different jurisdictions apply differing interest compounding mechanics. Canadian mortgages use semi-annual statutory compounding, while United States loans typically compound monthly. With our Mortgage Amortization Schedule Calculator and Mortgage Affordability Calculator , you can evaluate your qualifying income thresholds and compare payoff strategies before committing to a lender agreement.

# Frequently Asked Questions
# 1. How much mortgage can I get based on my income?
Your mortgage qualification limit depends on your gross household income, monthly debt obligations, and down payment. Lenders typically prefer a debt-to-income (DTI) ratio under 36% to 43%.
# 2. How does the home loan rate of interest affect payments?
Even small 0.5% rate shifts compound significantly over a 25 or 30-year term. Reviewing our interactive charts reveals how early payment cycles are primarily allocated to lender interest charges before equity accrues.
# 3. What is included in this mortgage loan repayment calculator?
Our calculator delivers complete monthly principal and interest figures, estimated taxes, homeowner insurance, HOA assessments, and comprehensive amortization tables.
# 4. Can extra principal payments shorten my loan term?
Yes. Direct principal prepayments bypass future interest accumulation entirely, drastically reducing loan tenure and cumulative interest expense.
How to use this calculator Work through the inputs in order and the results update instantly. Here is what each field means and where to find a realistic number.

chunks.title: Global Mortgage Calculator | Free Loan Payment Estimator
chunks.text:
Location & Currency. Choose your country first. This sets the currency symbol and the correct compounding convention: US loans compound monthly, Canadian mortgages use statutory semi-annual compounding, and UK and Australian loans follow their own market conventions. Comparing a US quote against a Canadian one without this switch will give you the wrong payment.
Loan amount. Enter the amount you actually borrow — the home price minus your down payment — not the purchase price. For a $500,000 home with 20% down, the loan amount is $400,000.
Interest rate. Your annual nominal rate, exactly as shown on the lender's Loan Estimate. Even a 0.25% difference changes a 30-year payment by roughly $17 per $100,000 borrowed, so use the locked or quoted rate, not a national average.
Term. The repayment period in years. Thirty years gives the lowest payment; 15 or 20 years cost more per month but slash lifetime interest dramatically.
Payment frequency. Monthly is the default. If your lender offers biweekly or accelerated biweekly schedules, switch here to see how 26 half-payments a year shorten the loan.

chunks.title: Global Mortgage Calculator | Free Loan Payment Estimator
chunks.text:
Property tax (annual). Enter the full yearly bill, not the monthly slice — the calculator divides it for you. US effective rates average around 1.1% of home value but range from under 0.5% to over 2% by county; your county assessor's site has the exact figure.
Home insurance (annual). Your yearly homeowner's premium. A typical US policy runs roughly $1,200–$2,400 per year depending on state and coverage; use your insurer's quote when you have one.
HOA / Condo fees (monthly). Any mandatory association dues. These never build equity, so buyers comparing a condo against a house should always include them — a $350 monthly HOA has the same budget impact as borrowing roughly $55,000 more at 6.5%.
Extra monthly payment (optional). Any additional amount you plan to send toward principal each month. The banner above the charts instantly shows the interest saved and years cut off, which makes this the fastest way to test payoff strategies.
# Understanding your results
Estimated payment / month. Your all-in housing cost: principal and interest plus property tax, insurance, and HOA. This is the number to compare against your take-home pay, not the P&I figure alone.

chunks.title: Global Mortgage Calculator | Free Loan Payment Estimator
chunks.text:
Principal & interest only. The pure loan payment. Lenders quote this figure; your budget needs the bigger one.
Property tax, Home insurance, HOA / fees. The monthly slices of each recurring cost, shown separately so you can see which non-loan cost dominates your payment.
Total principal & Total interest. What you borrow versus what the loan costs you over its full life. On a typical 30-year loan at 6–7%, total interest exceeds the amount borrowed — the single most eye-opening pair of numbers on this page.
Payoff in. How long until you own the home free and clear at the current settings. Add an extra payment and watch this number fall.
Extra-payment savings banner. Appears when you enter an extra monthly amount: dollars of interest avoided and years removed from the term.
Charts and amortization schedule. The annual breakdown shows the slow early shift from interest to principal; the full table lists every payment's split, so you can see exactly when your equity starts compounding in your favor.

Because the down payment is 20%, no private mortgage insurance is needed. Notice that the tax and insurance add $400 — about 14% — on top of the loan payment itself, which is why budgeting on P&I alone understates the true cost of ownership.
# Frequently asked questions
# Should I enter the home price or the loan amount?
Enter the loan amount: the purchase price minus your down payment. Entering the full home price overstates your payment and your lifetime interest, because you never borrow the down-payment portion.
# Which payment frequency should I choose?

chunks.title: Global Mortgage Calculator | Free Loan Payment Estimator
chunks.text:
Choose the frequency you will actually pay. Monthly matches most US billing. Biweekly creates 26 half-payments a year — the equivalent of 13 monthly payments — which quietly shaves years off the term, but only if your servicer applies the extra half-payment to principal.
# Why does the calculator ask for my location?
Compounding rules differ by country. A Canadian mortgage at a quoted 6% does not cost the same as a US mortgage at 6%, because Canada compounds semi-annually by statute while the US compounds monthly. Setting the location keeps the math honest.
# How close will this estimate be to my lender's quote?
Very close on principal and interest — the amortization math is standardized. The variables are your inputs: property tax assessments, insurance quotes, and HOA dues change the total. Treat the P&I as precise and the tax and insurance lines as well-researched estimates until you have actual bills.
# How do I compare a 15-year and a 30-year loan here?

chunks.title: Global Mortgage Calculator | Free Loan Payment Estimator
chunks.text:
Run the same loan amount and rate twice, changing only the term. A 15-year term roughly doubles the principal portion of each payment but typically cuts lifetime interest by more than half. Compare the "Total interest" lines side by side — that gap is the true price of the lower payment.
# Do I need to include property tax and insurance in my budget?
Yes. Lenders escrow them and most borrowers pay them as part of the monthly mortgage bill. A budget built on principal and interest alone can understate housing costs by 20–30% in high-tax areas.

chunks.title: FHA Loan Calculator – Payment with MIP Estimator
chunks.text:
Estimate your FHA monthly payment including upfront and annual mortgage insurance premium (MIP).
Estimate My FHA Payment
# FHA loans: the 3.5% down path to homeownership
FHA loans are insured by the Federal Housing Administration and designed for buyers who cannot put 20% down. The headline feature is the minimum down payment: just 3.5% with a credit score of 580 or higher (borrowers scoring 500–579 must put 10% down). That low barrier is why FHA backs a large share of first-time purchases. The tradeoff is mortgage insurance premium — MIP — which every FHA borrower pays in two forms, and which is generally more expensive over time than conventional PMI.
# Two kinds of MIP: upfront and annual

chunks.title: FHA Loan Calculator – Payment with MIP Estimator
chunks.text:
The upfront MIP is 1.75% of the base loan amount, and almost everyone finances it into the loan rather than paying cash — so a $337,750 loan becomes $343,661 before the first payment. The annual MIP is 0.55% of the loan balance per year for most borrowers (0.15% on 15-year loans at 90% LTV or below), divided into monthly installments. On that same loan, annual MIP adds about $157.51 a month. Unlike conventional PMI, the annual MIP rate does not improve with a higher credit score — it is the same for every FHA borrower in the same loan category.
# How long MIP lasts — the key FHA tradeoff
Here is the catch that surprises many buyers: with less than 10% down, FHA annual MIP lasts for the life of the loan — all 30 years, totaling over $56,000 on the example above. Put 10% or more down and MIP ends after 11 years instead. Conventional PMI, by contrast, drops off automatically at 78% loan-to-value. That is why borrowers who expect their home to appreciate often plan to refinance out of FHA into a conventional loan once they reach 20% equity — the MIP savings usually dwarf the refinance costs.
# What is FHA mortgage insurance (MIP)?

chunks.title: FHA Loan Calculator – Payment with MIP Estimator
chunks.text:
MIP is the FHA’s version of mortgage insurance, paid by every FHA borrower. It has two parts: an upfront premium of 1.75% of the loan (usually financed into the loan) and an annual premium — typically 0.55% of the balance — paid monthly with your mortgage payment.
# How much is the upfront MIP?
1.75% of the base loan amount. On a $337,750 loan that is $5,910.63, which is added to the loan balance, making the financed total $343,660.63. You pay interest on that amount too, which is why the financed option costs more than paying it in cash at closing.
# When does FHA MIP drop off?
With less than 10% down, annual MIP lasts for the life of the loan — it never drops off on its own. With 10% or more down, it ends after 11 years (132 payments). Many borrowers refinance into a conventional loan once they reach 20% equity to escape MIP entirely.
# FHA vs. conventional — which is cheaper?

chunks.title: FHA Loan Calculator – Payment with MIP Estimator
chunks.text:
It depends on your timeline. FHA usually wins for buyers with small down payments and weaker credit, thanks to lenient approval and low down payment requirements. But conventional PMI drops off at 78% loan-to-value while FHA MIP with less than 10% down lasts forever — so for buyers who will build equity quickly, conventional is often cheaper long-term. Compare both with our calculators.
# What credit score do I need for an FHA loan?
A score of 580 or higher qualifies for the minimum 3.5% down payment. Scores of 500–579 can still qualify but require 10% down. Below 500, FHA financing is generally not available — focus on credit repair first.

chunks.title: PMI Calculator – Private Mortgage Insurance Cost Estimator
chunks.text:
Estimate your monthly private mortgage insurance, when it drops off, and what it costs over the life of the loan.
# What is PMI and when is it required?
Private mortgage insurance protects the lender — not you — if you default on a conventional loan with a small down payment. Lenders require it whenever your loan-to-value ratio exceeds 80%, i.e., whenever you put down less than 20%. PMI typically costs between 0.3% and 0.85% of the loan amount per year, paid monthly on top of your principal and interest. On a $360,000 loan at 90% LTV, that is roughly $195 a month at typical rates. It is a pure cost of borrowing with a small down payment: unlike your loan payment, it builds no equity and earns you nothing.
# The 80/78 rule: how PMI drops off

chunks.title: PMI Calculator – Private Mortgage Insurance Cost Estimator
chunks.text:
PMI is not forever. Under federal law, you can request cancellation once your balance falls to 80% of the home’s original value — you must ask, and you need to be current on payments. Even if you forget, your servicer must terminate PMI automatically when the balance is scheduled to reach 78% of the original value. On a typical 30-year loan with 10% down at 6.5%, that automatic drop-off arrives around month 109 — roughly nine years in. Extra principal payments accelerate both dates, which is one of the highest-return uses of extra payments: every month of PMI avoided is pure savings on top of the interest saved.
# What PMI costs: rate tiers
PMI pricing is risk-based. Borrowers at 80–85% LTV might pay around 0.30% per year, while those above 95% LTV can pay 0.85% or more — and your credit score moves you within those bands. This calculator uses standard published tiers as estimates; your lender’s actual quote depends on your credit profile, occupancy, and property type. When comparing lenders, compare the PMI rate alongside the interest rate: a slightly higher rate with cheaper PMI can beat a lower rate with expensive PMI.
# What is PMI and why do lenders require it?

chunks.title: PMI Calculator – Private Mortgage Insurance Cost Estimator
chunks.text:
Private mortgage insurance protects the lender against default on conventional loans with less than 20% down. It lets borrowers buy sooner with a small down payment, at the cost of a monthly premium until the loan-to-value ratio drops to 80% or below.
# How much does PMI cost per month?
Typically 0.3% to 0.85% of the loan amount per year, divided into monthly payments. At 90% LTV, expect roughly 0.65% annually — about $195 a month on a $360,000 loan. Your credit score and exact LTV move the rate within that range.
# When does PMI automatically drop off?
Your servicer must cancel PMI automatically when your balance is scheduled to reach 78% of the home’s original value, provided you are current on payments. You can also request cancellation earlier, at 80% of original value.
# Can I avoid PMI without 20% down?
Yes, with tradeoffs. Piggyback loans (an 80-10-10 structure) keep the first mortgage at 80% LTV but add a second loan at a higher rate. Lender-paid mortgage insurance eliminates the monthly premium but usually means a higher interest rate. Run both options here before deciding.
# Is PMI tax-deductible?

chunks.title: PMI Calculator – Private Mortgage Insurance Cost Estimator
chunks.text: The federal deduction for mortgage insurance premiums has expired and been extended multiple times by Congress, so its current status depends on the tax year. Consult a tax advisor for the law in effect when you file.

chunks.title: DTI Calculator – Debt-to-Income Ratio
chunks.text:
Compute your front-end and back-end debt-to-income ratios — the numbers mortgage lenders use to qualify you.
# What is DTI? Front-end vs. back-end
Your debt-to-income ratio is the share of your gross monthly income consumed by debt payments. Lenders look at two versions. The front-end ratio counts only housing costs — principal, interest, property tax, homeowner’s insurance, and HOA dues (PITI). The back-end ratio adds every other recurring debt: car loans, student loans, credit-card minimums, personal loans, and child support. A borrower can pass the front-end test and fail the back-end one, which is why lenders always compute both.
# The 28/36 rule and the 43% QM ceiling
The textbook guideline is 28/36: no more than 28% of gross income on housing, no more than 36% on all debts combined. In practice, most conventional lenders approve back-end ratios up to 43–45% for borrowers with strong credit, cash reserves, or a large down payment, and FHA/VA programs go higher still. But the further past 36% you go, the thinner your margin for everything the ratio ignores — taxes, groceries, savings, and emergencies.
# How to lower your DTI before applying

chunks.title: DTI Calculator – Debt-to-Income Ratio
chunks.text:
You cannot change your income overnight, so attack the numerator: pay off a car loan, eliminate credit-card minimums, or choose a less expensive home to shrink the housing payment. Avoid opening new credit or financing furniture before closing — a new $400 monthly payment on a $10,000 monthly income adds 4 full points to your back-end ratio, which can kill an approval at the margin.
# What is a good debt-to-income ratio?
Under 36% back-end is considered strong by most lenders, and under 28% front-end keeps housing comfortable. Between 36% and 43% is approvable with compensating factors; above 43% is difficult for conventional loans.
# What is the difference between front-end and back-end DTI?
Front-end DTI is housing costs divided by gross monthly income. Back-end DTI is all monthly debt payments — including housing — divided by gross monthly income. Lenders evaluate both.
# Do lenders use gross or net income for DTI?
Gross — your pre-tax income. This flatters the ratio slightly, since taxes never appear in it. Always sanity-check the resulting payment against your actual take-home pay before committing.
# Can I get a mortgage with a 50% DTI?

chunks.title: DTI Calculator – Debt-to-Income Ratio
chunks.text:
Rarely through conventional channels — 43% is the qualified-mortgage ceiling most lenders observe. Some FHA, VA, or non-QM programs allow higher ratios with strong compensating factors, usually at higher rates.
# Do utilities and groceries count in my DTI?
No. DTI counts only debt obligations — loan payments, minimums, and support orders. Utilities, groceries, subscriptions, and discretionary spending are invisible to the ratio, which is exactly why your budget must be stricter than your DTI.

chunks.title: Rent vs Buy Calculator – Should You Rent or Buy?
chunks.text:
# Rent vs Buy Calculator
Compare the true long-term cost of renting vs. buying — including appreciation, rent hikes, equity, and what the renter could earn investing instead.
# Compare net wealth, not monthly payments
The monthly payment comparison misleads: buying looks expensive because the down payment and principal are “costs,” yet principal builds equity you keep. The honest comparison is net wealth after your planned stay. The buyer ends with home equity (value minus remaining balance minus selling costs); the renter ends with whatever the down payment and monthly savings grew to when invested. Whichever pile is bigger wins — and the answer flips with time horizon, appreciation, and rent growth.
A quick sanity check from the NYT framework: unrecoverable buying costs run about 5% of the home price per year — roughly 3% for the opportunity cost of tied-up capital, plus property tax and maintenance. If 5% of the price exceeds your annual rent, renting is likely cheaper; if rent is higher, buying usually wins. On a $400,000 home, 5% is $20,000 a year — versus $24,000 in rent at $2,000 a month, which points toward buying.

chunks.title: Rent vs Buy Calculator – Should You Rent or Buy?
chunks.text:
No calculator prices stability against mobility. Buying locks in your housing cost (minus tax and insurance drift) and lets you renovate freely — but selling within a few years usually loses to transaction costs of ~6–10%. Renting keeps you mobile and maintenance-free, but exposes you to rent hikes and forced moves. Treat the verdict as a financial baseline, then weigh the lifestyle factors the numbers cannot see.
# Is renting just throwing money away?
No — rent buys shelter, flexibility, and freedom from maintenance, taxes, and interest. The “throwing money away” framing ignores that early mortgage payments are mostly interest, which is equally unrecoverable. What matters is which path leaves you wealthier at the end, and that depends on your time horizon.
# How long do I need to stay for buying to beat renting?
Typically 5–7 years in a normal market, because buying’s upfront costs (down payment, closing, selling fees) need time to be overtaken by equity buildup and appreciation. In hot markets it can be 3–4 years; in flat markets, a decade or more.
# What is the 5% rule for rent vs. buy?

chunks.title: Rent vs Buy Calculator – Should You Rent or Buy?
chunks.text:
Multiply the home price by 5% — the approximate annual unrecoverable cost of owning (opportunity cost of capital, property tax, maintenance). If that exceeds your annual rent, renting is probably cheaper; if rent is higher, buying usually wins.
# Does home appreciation matter more than the mortgage rate?
Over long horizons, yes — appreciation compounds on the entire home value while you only borrowed most of it, so leverage magnifies it. But appreciation is uncertain and local; the mortgage rate is certain. Never buy counting on appreciation alone.
# Should I buy if I might move in 3 years?
Usually not. Selling costs of ~6% plus closing costs on both ends rarely get recovered in 3 years unless the market surges. Renting keeps your options open — run this calculator with 3 years to see your specific numbers.

chunks.title: Mortgage Extra Payment Calculator: 4 Ways to Pay Off Early
chunks.text:
# Mortgage Extra Payment Calculator: Early Payoff Savings
# Extra Contribution Strategy
# How Does Our Mortgage Extra Payment Calculator Work?
Every standard mortgage installment consists of two components: the principal debt and the lender's interest charge. When using our mortgage extra payment calculator , you can observe how contributing additional funds directly toward your principal balance reduces lifetime borrowing costs. Because regular amortizing loans calculate interest based on your remaining balance, reducing that balance early yields compounding financial benefits over time.
To evaluate baseline numbers before applying extra payments, check your amortization baseline using our Mortgage Amortization Schedule Calculator or verify your maximum borrowing power with our Mortgage Affordability Calculator .
# 4 Strategic Ways to Make Extra Mortgage Payments
Fixed Extra Monthly Payment: Adding an extra $50, $100, or $200 directly to your monthly payment slip is the most sustainable approach. Use the mortgage extra payment calculator above to see how small amounts eliminate multiple years of repayment.

chunks.title: Mortgage Extra Payment Calculator: 4 Ways to Pay Off Early
chunks.text:
Annual Lump-Sum Contributions: Directing tax refunds, work bonuses, or inheritance funds toward the principal once per year substantially suppresses interest compounding.
Accelerated Bi-Weekly Payments: Dividing your monthly mortgage installment by two and paying every two weeks creates 26 half-payments annually. This equates to 13 full payments each year, shaving between 4 to 6 years off a 30-year term without changing your monthly budget.
Loan Recasting or Refinancing Paydown: Paying a lump sum and having the lender recalculate your monthly bill without changing the interest rate. You can compare baseline structures using our primary Global Mortgage Loan Calculator .
# The Compounding Impact of Extra Payments: 30-Year Case Study

# Prepayment Penalties & Lender Guidelines

chunks.title: Mortgage Extra Payment Calculator: 4 Ways to Pay Off Early
chunks.text:
Before submitting extra funds, check with your lender or loan servicer to confirm that additional payments are applied directly to the principal curtailment rather than future scheduled payments. Furthermore, under federal lending rules monitored by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) , most conforming residential mortgages in the USA and Canada carry no prepayment penalties, allowing borrowers to pay down balances at their own pace.
# Frequently Asked Questions
Does an extra mortgage payment reduce principal or interest? When properly designated with your lender, any payment made in addition to your standard installment goes 100% toward lowering the principal balance.
Is it better to pay extra monthly or once a year? Paying extra monthly is slightly more advantageous because interest accrues continuously on your unpaid balance. Reducing the principal earlier lowers the balance subjected to compounding each billing period.

chunks.title: Mortgage Extra Payment Calculator: 4 Ways to Pay Off Early
chunks.text:
Can I use this mortgage extra payment calculator for UK and Canadian loans? Yes. Although Canadian mortgages use semi-annual compounding while UK and US loans calculate interest on monthly or daily balances, this mortgage extra payment calculator provides an accurate estimate of total debt reduction and accelerated payoff time across all major currencies.
# How to use this calculator
Enter your loan first, then layer on the extra-payment strategy you want to test. Each strategy below the form corresponds to one of the four approaches in the guide above.
Loan amount. Your current balance (or the original amount for a new loan) — extra-payment math is most dramatic on large, fresh balances.
Interest rate. Your contract rate. Higher rates make extra payments more valuable: each prepaid dollar avoids interest at this rate for the rest of the term.
Extra monthly payment. A fixed additional amount with every payment — $100, $200, whatever your budget sustains. This models strategy #1 and is the most powerful sustainable option because it compounds from month one.

chunks.title: Mortgage Extra Payment Calculator: 4 Ways to Pay Off Early
chunks.text:
Extra annual payment. A once-a-year lump sum — a tax refund, bonus, or inheritance (strategy #2). Annual lump sums help, but the same dollars spread monthly save slightly more, because interest accrues every month on the unpaid balance.
For the biweekly approach (strategy #3), divide your monthly payment by two and pay it every two weeks — the 26 half-payments equal 13 full payments a year. For recasting (strategy #4), model the lump sum here, then ask your servicer for a recast quote to see the new lower payment.
# Understanding your results
Standard Monthly Installment. Your baseline P&I with no extras — the reference point for everything below.
New Accelerated Payment. Baseline plus your extra amount: the actual check you will write each month.
Original Total Interest vs. New Total Interest. The lifetime interest with and without the strategy. The gap between them is the headline savings — often larger than the total of the extra payments themselves, because each prepaid dollar avoids years of compounding.
Total Interest Saved. The gap, stated directly: dollars you keep instead of paying the lender.

chunks.title: Mortgage Extra Payment Calculator: 4 Ways to Pay Off Early
chunks.text:
Time Saved (Payoff Early By). Years and months removed from the term. This is the freedom metric — the date your housing payment drops to just taxes and insurance.
New Loan Payoff Date. The month you become mortgage-free under the strategy. Circle it: it is the most motivating number on the page.
A $350,000 mortgage at 6.50% for 30 years with an extra $200/month toward principal:
Standard payment: $2,212.24/month ; accelerated payment: $2,412.24/month
Baseline: 360 months (30.0 years), total interest $446,406
With +$200/month: payoff in 286 months (23.8 years) , total interest $338,309
Interest saved: $108,097 — time saved: 6.2 years
The $200 monthly extras total about $57,200 over the shortened term, yet they eliminate $108,097 of interest — nearly double the outlay — because every early dollar avoids interest charges for up to 24 remaining years. That asymmetry is the entire case for prepayment.
# Frequently asked questions
# Should I pay extra on my mortgage or invest the money instead?

chunks.title: Mortgage Extra Payment Calculator: 4 Ways to Pay Off Early
chunks.text:
Compare after-tax returns: prepaying a 6.50% mortgage earns a risk-free, tax-free 6.50% on every dollar. Investing might beat that over decades, but with market risk and taxes. The tiebreakers are liquidity (investments stay accessible; home equity does not) and psychology — many borrowers happily accept the lower "return" of a paid-off house.
# What is mortgage recasting, and how is it different from prepaying?
Recasting keeps your rate and term but re-amortizes the loan after a lump-sum payment, lowering the required monthly payment for a small fee (often a few hundred dollars). Prepaying without recasting keeps the payment the same and shortens the term instead. Choose recasting for monthly relief, plain prepayment for maximum interest savings.
# Do I need to tell my lender the extra money is for principal?
Yes — explicitly, and in writing. Some servicers default extra funds to "future payments" or escrow, which earns you nothing. Designate every extra payment as "principal curtailment" (most servicers have a checkbox or memo field), then verify on the next statement that the balance dropped accordingly.
# Is there a minimum extra payment worth making?

chunks.title: Mortgage Extra Payment Calculator: 4 Ways to Pay Off Early
chunks.text:
There is no threshold — the math is linear, so even $25/month on a fresh 30-year loan saves thousands over time. The practical minimum is whatever you will sustain: an extra $50 you pay for ten years beats an extra $300 you abandon after six months.
# Can extra payments remove PMI faster?
Yes, and this is one of the highest-return uses of extra payments. Conventional PMI typically drops at 80% loan-to-value (and auto-terminates at 78%). Directing extras at the principal can pull that date forward by years — run the numbers, because each month of PMI avoided is pure savings on top of the interest saved.
# What if I cannot keep up the extra payments later?
Nothing bad happens. Extra payments are voluntary — unlike a 15-year refinance, which locks in the higher payment. If income drops, simply stop the extras and the loan reverts to its original schedule. That reversibility is the strategic advantage of prepaying a 30-year loan over refinancing into a shorter term.

When Does Refinancing Make Financial Sense?

Frequently Asked Questions
# How Does a Mortgage Refinance Calculator Work?
Refinancing involves replacing your existing home mortgage with a new debt instrument that carries updated terms, a revised interest rate, and a new repayment horizon. Using our mortgage refinance calculator allows you to evaluate whether interest reductions outweigh mandatory upfront origination fees, appraisal costs, and closing expenses.
Before proceeding with a refinance, compare your current multi-year debt payoff using our Mortgage Amortization Schedule Calculator or explore accelerated payoff alternatives via our Mortgage Extra Payment Calculator .
# Understanding the Refinance Break-Even Formula
The single most crucial metric when evaluating a refinance is the break-even period . This is the exact number of months required for your monthly interest savings to fully recoup your upfront closing fees:

chunks.title: Mortgage Refinance Calculator: Break-Even & Monthly Savings
chunks.text:
Break-Even Horizon (Months) = Total Refinance Closing Costs ÷ Monthly Payment Reduction
For example, if your lender charges $4,000 in closing costs and your new rate reduces your payment by $200 per month, your break-even horizon is exactly 20 months. If you plan to remain in your home longer than 20 months, the refinance creates net positive financial value. Our mortgage refinance calculator computes this equation instantly.
# When Does Refinancing Make Financial Sense?
Interest Rates Drop by 0.75% or More: Historically, reducing your contract rate by at least 75 to 100 basis points produces meaningful savings.
Shortening Your Loan Horizon: Transitioning from a 30-year mortgage to a 15-year term drastically cuts lifetime compounding charges.
Eliminating Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI): If your home equity has exceeded 20%, refinancing into a conventional mortgage can remove expensive monthly insurance premiums.
Converting from ARM to Fixed: Switching from an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage to a stable fixed-rate product guarantees payment security. You can model base options using our Global Mortgage Loan Calculator .
# Underwriting Fees & Consumer Guidance

chunks.title: Mortgage Refinance Calculator: Break-Even & Monthly Savings
chunks.text:
Under disclosure regulations established by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) , lenders must deliver a Loan Estimate within three business days of application. Compare title insurance, origination points, and appraisal costs against the projections in this mortgage refinance calculator to ensure you receive favorable terms.
# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is a good break-even period for refinancing?
A break-even period under 24 to 36 months is generally considered excellent for homeowners planning to stay in their property medium to long term.
# Can I roll closing costs into the new loan balance?
Yes. Many lenders offer "no-cost" or rolled-in refinancing, which finances closing costs into the loan balance in exchange for a slightly higher balance or interest rate.
# Does refinancing reset my amortization term?
Yes, unless you choose a shorter term (like 15 or 20 years). If you are 5 years into a 30-year mortgage and refinance into a new 30-year term, your overall payoff timeline extends to 35 years.
# How to use this calculator

chunks.title: Mortgage Refinance Calculator: Break-Even & Monthly Savings
chunks.text:
Describe the loan you have and the loan you are considering. The calculator reduces the decision to two numbers: monthly savings and the breakeven horizon.
Current loan balance. The payoff amount on your latest statement — not the original loan. Refinancing math runs on what you owe today.
Current interest rate. Your existing note rate. Pull it from the note itself; many borrowers misremember it by a quarter point, which swings the savings materially.
Remaining term. Years left on the current loan. This is the input most people get wrong: entering 30 when only 24 remain makes the refinance look better than it is, because it hides the amortization restart.
New interest rate. The quoted or hypothetical replacement rate. Meaningful savings historically start around 0.75–1% below your current rate, though large balances can justify smaller improvements.
New loan term. Usually 30 years, but test 20 or 15: a shorter term raises the payment while collapsing lifetime interest, and the calculator shows both effects.

chunks.title: Mortgage Refinance Calculator: Break-Even & Monthly Savings
chunks.text:
Closing costs. All-in settlement charges — origination, appraisal, title, prepaids — typically 2–5% of the loan. The Loan Estimate your lender must deliver within three business days of application itemizes every dollar.
# Understanding your results
Current Monthly Payment. Your existing P&I, recomputed from your inputs as a consistency check against your statement.
New Monthly Payment. The proposed P&I at the new rate and term.
Monthly Savings. The payment reduction — your monthly "gain," which only becomes real profit after closing costs are recovered.
Break-Even Horizon. Closing costs ÷ monthly savings, in months. Under 24–36 months is generally excellent for homeowners staying put; beyond 48 months, weigh your moving plans carefully.
Total Lifetime Interest Savings. Interest under the old loan minus interest under the new one, over the full terms. Read it net of closing costs, and remember it assumes you keep the loan to maturity — selling early forfeits the tail of the savings.
A borrower owes $300,000 at 7.50% with 30 years left and is offered 6.25% for 30 years with $7,500 in closing costs:
Current payment: $2,097.64/month
New payment: $1,847.15/month

chunks.title: Mortgage Refinance Calculator: Break-Even & Monthly Savings
chunks.text:
Monthly savings: $250.49
Breakeven: $7,500 ÷ $250.49 ≈ 30 months
Lifetime interest — current: $455,152; new: $364,975
Net lifetime benefit after closing costs: $82,677
The refinance pays for itself in two and a half years and nets over $80,000 across the full term — a clear win for anyone staying longer than the breakeven. If the same borrower instead chose a 15-year term at 5.75%, the payment would rise but lifetime interest would fall by roughly another $150,000: the classic payment-versus-wealth tradeoff the calculator lets you test.
# Frequently asked questions
# What credit score do I need to refinance?
Conventional rate-and-term refinances generally want 620+, with the best pricing reserved for 740+. FHA and VA streamline products are more forgiving — they exist precisely so borrowers can capture lower rates without a full credit re-underwrite. If your score has improved since you bought, that alone can justify running the numbers.
# Can I refinance an FHA loan into a conventional loan?

chunks.title: Mortgage Refinance Calculator: Break-Even & Monthly Savings
chunks.text:
Yes, and it is one of the highest-value refinances available: conventional loans drop mortgage insurance at 80% loan-to-value, while FHA mortgage insurance premium persists for the life of most FHA loans. Borrowers whose homes have appreciated into 20%+ equity often save twice — a lower rate plus no more MIP.
# Should I refinance into a 15-year term?
If the higher payment fits comfortably — ideally under 28% of gross income — the 15-year term is a wealth-building machine: lower rates plus half the amortization years typically cut lifetime interest by 60–70%. The risk is liquidity: the higher payment is mandatory, unlike voluntary extra payments on a 30-year loan.
# How soon after buying can I refinance?
For a conventional rate-and-term refinance, there is no mandatory waiting period — you can refinance the month after purchase if rates justify it. Cash-out refinances typically require six months of ownership (the "seasoning" period), and you will need a new appraisal reflecting any value change.
# Does refinancing affect my property taxes?

chunks.title: Mortgage Refinance Calculator: Break-Even & Monthly Savings
chunks.text:
No. Refinancing replaces the loan, not the ownership — your tax assessment, exemptions, and payment schedule are untouched. The only interaction is indirect: some borrowers escrow differently after refinancing, which changes the monthly impound amount but never the tax itself.
# Fixed or ARM for a refinance — which should I choose?
Match the product to your horizon. Staying 7+ years: fixed rate, for payment certainty. Selling or expecting rates to fall within 5 years: a 5/1 or 7/1 ARM's lower initial rate can win — but model the worst-case adjusted payment, not just the teaser rate, before committing.

chunks.title: Paycheck Calculator – Take-Home Pay Estimator
chunks.text:
Estimate your 2026 take-home pay after federal tax, FICA, state tax and deductions.
Calculate Take-Home Pay
# How your paycheck is calculated
Your gross salary is only the starting point. Before money reaches your bank account, several layers are removed: pre-tax deductions (like 401(k) contributions and HSA deposits), FICA payroll taxes, federal income tax, state income tax, and any post-tax deductions. What remains is your take-home pay. For 2026, the standard deduction is $16,100 for single filers, $32,200 for married couples filing jointly, and $24,150 for heads of household.
# Pre-tax vs. post-tax deductions
Pre-tax deductions lower both your taxable wages and your FICA wages, so every $1,000 into a traditional 401(k) saves roughly $220 in federal tax (at the 22% bracket) plus $76.50 in FICA. Post-tax deductions come out after taxes with no tax benefit.
# Why take-home differs from salary ÷ pay periods
The gap comes from progressive taxation plus flat payroll taxes of 7.65% on the first $184,500 of wages. High earners face 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax above $200,000 (single) or $250,000 (joint). State taxes widen the gap further.

chunks.title: Paycheck Calculator – Take-Home Pay Estimator
chunks.text:
# Why is my take-home pay so much less than my salary?
Federal income tax, 7.65% FICA payroll taxes, state income tax, and benefit deductions combine to 25–35% of gross pay for typical earners.
6.2% for Social Security (on wages up to $184,500 in 2026) plus 1.45% for Medicare on all wages.
# Does state income tax really matter?
Yes — nine states have no income tax while others charge over 10%. A 5% rate on $80,000 costs $4,000 a year.
# How do pre-tax deductions help?
They reduce wages subject to income tax and FICA. A $5,000 401(k) at the 22% bracket saves about $1,483 a year.
# Is this accurate for 2026?
It uses verified 2026 IRS figures. It is an estimate — your employer’s payroll system determines exact withholding.
# How to use this calculator
Enter your pay details top to bottom; each layer is subtracted in the order your employer’s payroll system applies them.
Gross salary. Your annual pay before anything is removed. Hourly workers: multiply your hourly rate by hours per week × 52.

chunks.title: Paycheck Calculator – Take-Home Pay Estimator
chunks.text:
Pay frequency. Weekly (52), biweekly (26), semi-monthly (24), or monthly (12). This only changes the per-check figures — annual totals are identical — but it determines the number you actually see hit your bank account.
Filing status. Used for the federal income-tax calculation: single, married filing jointly, or head of household. It selects your standard deduction ($16,100 / $32,200 / $24,150 for 2026) and bracket thresholds.
State income tax rate. Enter your state’s flat rate as a percentage (0 if your state has none). Nine states levy no income tax at all; others charge over 10%. On an $80,000 salary, a 5% state rate costs $4,000 a year — the single biggest geographic swing in take-home pay.
Pre-tax deductions. Traditional 401(k) contributions, HSA deposits, and pre-tax health premiums. These reduce the wages subject to both income tax and FICA, so they are the highest-value line on the form: $5,000 into a 401(k) at the 22% bracket saves about $1,100 in federal tax plus $382.50 in FICA — $1,482.50 a year.
Post-tax deductions. Roth 401(k) contributions, union dues, or garnishments taken after taxes. They reduce take-home dollar for dollar with no tax benefit.

chunks.title: Paycheck Calculator – Take-Home Pay Estimator
chunks.text:
# Understanding your results
Gross pay per paycheck. Salary divided by pay periods — the starting line before any subtraction.
Federal income tax. Withholding computed from your taxable wages through the 2026 brackets. Note this is withholding, an estimate of your annual liability divided across checks; the final reckoning happens at filing time.
FICA — Social Security & Medicare. A flat 7.65% on wages up to the $184,500 Social Security wage base (6.2% Social Security + 1.45% Medicare on all wages). Unlike income tax, there is no standard deduction — FICA starts on dollar one.
State income tax. Your state’s share, the most variable line on the stub.
Net (take-home) pay. Per paycheck and annualized: the number your budget should actually be built on. For typical earners the combined bite of federal tax, FICA, state tax, and deductions lands between 25–35% of gross.
A single filer earning $100,000 , paid biweekly (26 checks) , in a state with no income tax and no extra deductions:
Gross per paycheck: $100,000 ÷ 26 = $3,846.15
Federal income tax: $13,170/year (13.17% effective, per our 2026 figures) → $506.54 per check

chunks.title: Paycheck Calculator – Take-Home Pay Estimator
chunks.text:
FICA: Social Security 6.2% × $100,000 = $6,200 ($238.46/check) + Medicare 1.45% × $100,000 = $1,450 ($55.77/check) → $294.23 per check
Take-home: $79,180/year → $3,045.38 per paycheck
Now add a $5,000 pre-tax 401(k): taxable wages fall to $95,000, federal tax drops by about $1,100, FICA drops by $382.50 — the saver keeps $1,482.50 more of the $5,000 than it cost in take-home pay.
# Frequently asked questions
# Do bonuses get taxed at a higher rate?
Bonuses face a flat 22% federal supplemental withholding rate (not your marginal bracket), which is why a bonus check can feel heavily taxed. At filing time the bonus is simply part of your total income — if 22% was too much, you get the difference back as a refund.
# What is the Additional Medicare Tax — will I owe it?
An extra 0.9% on wages above $200,000 (single) or $250,000 (joint), withheld automatically once your pay crosses the threshold. There is no employer match on it, and unlike regular FICA it is not capped — very high earners pay it on every additional dollar.
# Can I adjust my W-4 to change my take-home pay?

chunks.title: Paycheck Calculator – Take-Home Pay Estimator
chunks.text:
Yes. The W-4 controls withholding, not your actual tax: claiming the right adjustments (or adding extra withholding per pay period) tunes each check toward your true liability. Owing a small amount in April means you gave the IRS an interest-free loan of zero — the efficient outcome, as long as you avoid underpayment penalties.
# What is the difference between salary and hourly inputs here?
None in the math — the calculator annualizes hourly pay (rate × hours × 52) before running the same tax layers. The only caveat: overtime and variable hours make any single paycheck an estimate, so hourly workers should treat the annual figure as the planning number.
# Are HSA contributions really triple tax-free?
Yes, when used correctly: contributions avoid income tax and FICA, growth is tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax-free — the only account with all three. The catch is you must be enrolled in a qualifying high-deductible health plan to contribute.

chunks.text:
# Mortgage Amortization Schedule Calculator
# Complete Amortization Breakdown
# How Does a Mortgage Amortization Calculator Work?
A mortgage amortization schedule is an essential actuarial framework that charts each monthly installment throughout the life of a fixed-rate loan. In the early stages of a 30-year or 15-year term, monthly payments are heavily weighted toward bank interest charges. As the principal balance diminishes, each subsequent installment directs greater funding directly toward property equity.
Using an intuitive mortgage amortization calculator allows borrowers to track this equity transition, evaluate compounding mechanics, and analyze the total interest obligation required before full homeownership is realized. For borrowers assessing their overall qualification limits before selecting a loan, pairing this tool with our Mortgage Affordability Calculator provides a complete income-to-debt perspective.
# Key Metrics Inside Your Mortgage Amortization Schedule
Principal Balance: The original loan amount borrowed from your financial institution minus cumulative debt payments made to date.

chunks.title: Mortgage Amortization Schedule Calculator (Monthly & Yearly)
chunks.text:
Periodic Interest Charge: The financing fee computed by multiplying your monthly interest rate by the remaining unpaid loan principal.
Total Installment: The mandatory monthly payment combining principal reduction and accrued lender interest.
Ending Balance: The remaining principal obligation carried forward into the subsequent billing cycle.
# 15-Year vs. 30-Year Mortgage Amortization Comparison
Comparing different amortization terms shows the dramatic impact of compounding frequency. The table below illustrates a standard $350,000 mortgage at a 6.50% interest rate:
While the 30-year term provides lower monthly cash flow requirements, a 15-year schedule saves more than $247,000 in compounding interest fees. To compare general regional interest rules and statutory compounding, you can also model variables with our core Global Mortgage Loan Calculator .
# Federal Regulations and Consumer Mortgage Guidance

chunks.title: Mortgage Amortization Schedule Calculator (Monthly & Yearly)
chunks.text:
Under official underwriting guidelines published by federal authorities such as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) , lenders must provide clear disclosure of total finance charges, annual percentage rates (APR), and mandatory escrow allocations before loan closing. Utilizing a verified mortgage amortization calculator ensures that your actual repayment schedule matches statutory disclosure documentation.
# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is a mortgage amortization calculator?
A mortgage amortization calculator is a financial tool that computes the exact monthly division of principal and interest over your loan term, generating a complete schedule from your first payment to final maturity.
# Why does my loan balance decline slowly in the first five years?
Because interest charges are calculated on your remaining balance, the highest interest fees occur when the loan balance is largest. Over time, as principal decreases, less interest accrues and equity builds rapidly.
# Can extra payments accelerate my amortization schedule?

chunks.title: Mortgage Amortization Schedule Calculator (Monthly & Yearly)
chunks.text:
Yes. Any additional capital applied directly to the loan principal immediately reduces the base upon which subsequent interest is calculated, shortening the overall loan tenure and lowering cumulative interest charges.
# How to use this calculator
Three inputs generate the entire schedule — every payment for the life of the loan. Precision here pays off everywhere else.
Loan amount. The principal you are borrowing (home price minus down payment). The schedule is linear in this input: doubling the loan doubles every payment and every interest total, so you can scale the results mentally.
Interest rate. The annual nominal rate. On a 30-year term, each 0.5% moves the monthly payment by roughly $30 per $100,000 — and moves lifetime interest by tens of thousands.
Term. The full amortization period in years — 30, 20, or 15 are standard. This single choice has the largest effect on the interest/principal split of your early payments.

chunks.title: Mortgage Amortization Schedule Calculator (Monthly & Yearly)
chunks.text:
The calculator then builds the schedule payment by payment: each month's interest equals the remaining balance times the monthly rate, and whatever is left of the fixed payment reduces principal. That one rule explains the entire shape of the table — and it is also why rounding your payment up to the nearest $50 or $100 has an outsized effect in the early years, when nearly the whole payment would otherwise go to interest.
# Understanding your results
Monthly Principal & Interest. Your fixed contractual payment, unchanged for the life of a fixed-rate loan.
Total Principal Repaid. Should equal your original loan amount — a useful checksum that the schedule is complete.
Total Interest Charged. The lifetime cost of borrowing. Compare this across terms before choosing: the gap between a 15-year and 30-year schedule is usually the largest number on the page.
Total Overall Payments. Principal plus interest: the full amount leaving your pocket over the loan's life, before taxes and insurance.
Payoff Date. The month of your final payment, counting from the assumed start. Useful for retirement planning — a 30-year loan started at 40 ends at 70.

chunks.title: Mortgage Amortization Schedule Calculator (Monthly & Yearly)
chunks.text:
Yearly schedule table. Each row shows the year's principal, interest, total paid, and ending balance. Read down the "Interest" column to watch it shrink and the "Principal" column to watch it grow — the crossover point, where principal first exceeds interest, is the moment your equity starts compounding in your favor.
A $400,000 loan at 6.75% for 30 years , paid monthly:
Monthly payment: $2,594.39 (fixed for all 360 payments)
Total interest over 30 years: $533,981
Payment #1: $2,250.00 interest + $344.39 principal — 87% of the first payment is interest
Payment #360: $0.09 interest + $2,594.30 principal — the mirror image
The same payment buys $2,250 of interest in month one and $2,594 of equity in month 360. That inversion is amortization in one picture — and it is why extra payments made early, when the interest slice is fattest, destroy the most lifetime interest per dollar.
# Frequently asked questions
# What is the difference between amortization and depreciation?

chunks.title: Mortgage Amortization Schedule Calculator (Monthly & Yearly)
chunks.text:
Amortization is a loan concept: spreading repayment across scheduled payments. Depreciation is an accounting concept: an asset losing value over time. Your house amortizes (the loan shrinks on schedule) while it may appreciate or depreciate in market value — the two move independently.
# How do I read the yearly table?
Each row is one year: "Principal" is equity gained that year, "Interest" is the lender's cut, and "Ending Balance" is what you still owe. Scan the Interest column downward — the year it drops below the Principal column is your crossover year, the single best summary of the schedule's shape.
# Does making one extra payment a year really help?
Yes, disproportionately. One extra monthly payment per year on a 30-year loan typically cuts 4–6 years off the term, because each extra dollar lands when the balance — and therefore the interest drag — is highest. Our Extra Payment Calculator models your exact loan.
# Can I get an amortization schedule from my lender?

chunks.title: Mortgage Amortization Schedule Calculator (Monthly & Yearly)
chunks.text:
Yes — servicers provide one on request, and your closing Truth in Lending disclosure includes the total-of-payments figure. Compare the lender's schedule against this calculator's; on a standard fixed-rate loan they should match to the cent, and any difference is worth a phone call.
# What happens to my schedule if I have an ARM and rates change?
The schedule recalculates at each adjustment: the remaining balance is re-amortized over the remaining term at the new rate, producing a new payment. Fixed-rate schedules never change; ARM schedules are a series of fixed-rate segments stitched together.
# How is a 15-year schedule different, besides being shorter?
The equity curve is far steeper: after 5 years on a 15-year loan you typically owe roughly 75% of the original balance, versus about 90% on a 30-year. That faster equity buildup is why 15-year borrowers can sell or refinance from strength much sooner.

chunks.title: Income Tax Calculator 2026 – Estimate Federal Tax
chunks.text:
# Income Tax Calculator
Estimate your federal income tax using official 2026 IRS brackets and deductions.
# Taxable income: the number that actually matters
Federal brackets apply to taxable income — gross income minus the standard deduction ($16,100 single, $32,200 joint, $24,150 head of household in 2026) or itemized deductions. A single earner making $100,000 is taxed on only $83,900.
# Marginal vs. effective tax rate
Your marginal rate is the tax on your last dollar (22% in the $100,000 example); your effective rate is total tax ÷ total income (13.17%). Only dollars above each threshold are taxed at the higher rate — never your entire income.
# Standard deduction in 2026
About 90% of taxpayers take the standard deduction. Itemizing only wins if mortgage interest, state/local taxes (capped at $10,000), and charitable gifts exceed the standard amount.
# What is the difference between marginal and effective tax rate?
Marginal is the rate on your next dollar; effective is total tax divided by total income. Your effective rate is always lower than your marginal rate.
# Should I take the standard deduction or itemize?

chunks.title: Income Tax Calculator 2026 – Estimate Federal Tax
chunks.text:
Take whichever is larger. For 2026, itemizing only wins if deductions exceed $16,100 single / $32,200 joint / $24,150 head of household.
# Does this include state income tax?
No — federal income tax only. State rates range from 0% to over 13%.
# What changed for 2026 vs. 2025?
Bracket thresholds, the standard deduction, and the Social Security wage base were adjusted upward for inflation. The 10%–37% structure is unchanged.
No. This is an educational estimate using published IRS figures. Consult a qualified tax professional for major decisions.
# How to use this calculator
Three inputs produce the full estimate. The calculator handles the bracket layering automatically — you never need to look up a tax table.
Gross annual income. Your total earnings before any deductions: salary, bonuses, freelance and business income combined. Enter the full-year figure, not per-paycheck.

chunks.title: Income Tax Calculator 2026 – Estimate Federal Tax
chunks.text:
Filing status. Single, married filing jointly, or head of household. This single choice changes everything downstream: the standard deduction ($16,100 single, $32,200 joint, $24,150 head of household for 2026), the bracket thresholds, and therefore the final bill. Married couples should model both “joint” and two “single” scenarios when deciding how to file.
Deduction type. Leave it on “Standard (automatic)” for the quick estimate, or switch to “Itemized” and enter your total itemized deductions (mortgage interest, state and local taxes up to the cap, charitable gifts). Itemizing only wins when your deductions beat the standard amount for your status.
The calculator first subtracts your deduction to reach taxable income — the only number the brackets actually touch. It then applies the 10%–37% brackets in layers (each rate taxes only the dollars inside its band), and reports both your marginal and effective rates. If the result shows you are significantly over- or under-withheld versus your employer’s payroll deductions, use it as the basis for filing a new W-4 — adjusting withholding during the year beats waiting for a refund or a bill in April.
# Understanding your results

chunks.title: Income Tax Calculator 2026 – Estimate Federal Tax
chunks.text:
Taxable income. Gross income minus your deduction (standard or itemized). This is the figure that determines your bracket placement — a $100,000 single earner taking the standard deduction is taxed on only $83,900.
Federal income tax. The estimated total liability for the year, computed layer by layer through the brackets.
Marginal tax rate. The rate on your next dollar of income — the number that matters for decisions like “should I do overtime?” or “is this deduction worth it?”
Effective tax rate. Total tax divided by gross income. Because of the layered brackets, this is always lower than your marginal rate — 13.17% versus 22% in the $100,000 example below — and it is the honest measure of your overall burden.
After-tax income. Gross minus federal tax: the starting point for your real budget before state tax and payroll taxes.
A single filer earning $100,000 in 2026, taking the standard deduction:
Standard deduction: $16,100 → taxable income: $83,900
Marginal rate: 22% (the rate on the last dollar earned)
Federal income tax: $13,170 (computed through the bracket layers)
Effective rate: $13,170 ÷ $100,000 = 13.17%
After federal tax: $86,830 — before state tax and FICA

chunks.title: Income Tax Calculator 2026 – Estimate Federal Tax
chunks.text:
Notice the gap between the 22% marginal and 13.17% effective rates: only the dollars above each threshold are taxed at the higher rate. A raise that pushes you “into the 24% bracket” taxes just the extra dollars at 24% — your existing income is untouched.
# Frequently asked questions
# Do I have to file a return if I earned very little?
Not always — filing thresholds roughly track the standard deduction, so a single filer under about $16,100 of gross income generally owes nothing and may not need to file. But file anyway if you had withholding: it is the only way to claim a refund, and low earners may qualify for refundable credits.
# What is the difference between a tax credit and a tax deduction?
A deduction shrinks the income being taxed (a $1,000 deduction saves $220 at the 22% bracket); a credit shrinks the tax bill dollar for dollar (a $1,000 credit saves $1,000). Credits are strictly more valuable — which is why the child tax credit and education credits get so much attention at filing time.
# Are Social Security benefits taxed?

chunks.title: Income Tax Calculator 2026 – Estimate Federal Tax
chunks.text:
They can be. Depending on your “combined income,” up to 85% of benefits become taxable at ordinary rates — which surprises many new retirees. The taxation of benefits is one reason Roth withdrawals (which do not count toward combined income) are so valuable in retirement planning.
# How can I legally lower my taxable income?
The big levers: pre-tax 401(k) and HSA contributions, deductible student-loan interest, and — if your itemized total beats the standard deduction — mortgage interest, state and local taxes (capped at $10,000), and charitable gifts. Each dollar shifted out of taxable income saves your marginal rate.
# When are 2026 federal taxes due?
April 2027, typically the 15th. Quarterly estimated payments apply if you owe significantly through freelance or investment income — the IRS charges penalties for under-withholding, so adjust W-4 withholding or pay estimates during the year rather than settling up in April.
# Does this calculator handle capital gains or rental income?

chunks.title: Income Tax Calculator 2026 – Estimate Federal Tax
chunks.text:
No — it models ordinary wage-like income through the standard brackets. Long-term capital gains, qualified dividends, and rental income follow separate rate schedules and rules, so treat this estimate as your baseline and consult the dedicated IRS worksheets for investment income.

chunks.title: Roth IRA Calculator – Project Tax-Free Growth
chunks.text:
Project tax-free retirement growth with 2026 IRS limits and compound returns.
# How a Roth IRA grows tax-free
A Roth IRA reverses the traditional retirement deal: you contribute after-tax dollars today, and every dollar of growth can be withdrawn tax-free in retirement. A 30-year-old contributing $7,000 a year at 7% could hold over $1 million tax-free by 65.
# 2026 contribution limits and phaseouts
For 2026: $7,500/year under 50, $8,600 at 50+. Phaseouts: $153,000–$168,000 MAGI (single), $242,000–$252,000 (joint). Above these, use the backdoor Roth strategy.
# Roth vs. Traditional IRA
Choose Roth when you expect higher taxes in retirement — typical for young professionals. Earnings are tax-free after 59½ once the account is five years old.
# How much can I contribute to a Roth IRA in 2026?
$7,500 under 50, $8,600 at 50+. The limit applies across all IRAs combined and cannot exceed earned income.
# What if I earn too much to contribute directly?
Above $168,000 single / $252,000 joint, use the backdoor Roth: nondeductible Traditional IRA contribution converted to Roth.
# When can I withdraw from a Roth IRA?

chunks.title: Roth IRA Calculator – Project Tax-Free Growth
chunks.text:
Contributions anytime, tax-free. Earnings tax-free after 59½ with the five-year rule met.
# Roth vs. Traditional IRA — which is better?
Roth wins if your tax rate will be higher in retirement; Traditional if you need the deduction today.
# Does my 401(k) match count toward the limit?
No. IRA and 401(k) limits are separate; employer matches never count against your IRA limit.
# How to use this calculator
Six inputs drive the whole projection. Small changes in the return assumption dominate the result, so spend most of your effort there. Contribution timing matters too: deposits made in January compound for nearly a full year longer than December deposits, so funding early in the year is a free, small boost the calculator assumes when you enter the full annual amount.
Current age. Your age today. Time is the most powerful input in the model — starting at 25 instead of 35 can nearly double the final balance at the same contribution.
Retirement age. When you plan to stop contributing and start withdrawing. Sixty-five is the standard benchmark; earlier retirement means fewer compounding years and a smaller balance.

chunks.title: Roth IRA Calculator – Project Tax-Free Growth
chunks.text:
Annual contribution. What you will invest each year. For 2026 the IRS caps this at $7,500 under age 50 and $8,600 at 50 and older, and the cap applies across all your IRAs combined — so do not model $7,500 here plus another $7,500 elsewhere.
Expected annual return. Your assumed average yearly growth, net of fees. Seven percent is the commonly used long-run planning figure for a stock-heavy portfolio; use 4–5% if your allocation is conservative. Every point changes the outcome by hundreds of thousands over 30+ years.
Current balance. What is already in the account today, if anything. Existing money compounds for the full remaining period, so even a small current balance moves the needle.
Filing status and MAGI (optional). If you enter your modified adjusted gross income, the calculator checks the 2026 Roth phaseout ($153,000–$168,000 single / head of household, $242,000–$252,000 joint) and warns you if your contribution needs reducing — or whether a backdoor Roth is your path.
# Understanding your results

chunks.title: Roth IRA Calculator – Project Tax-Free Growth
chunks.text:
Projected balance at retirement. The headline number: contributions plus compounded growth, all withdrawable tax-free in retirement provided you are 59½ and the five-year rule is met.
Total contributions. The sum of your out-of-pocket deposits. Comparing this against the projected balance shows how much of the final number is your money versus growth.
Total growth (earnings). The compounding payoff — the portion the IRS will never tax. In long-horizon scenarios this is typically two to three times the contributions, which is the entire economic case for the Roth.
Year-by-year projection. The growth curve steepens dramatically in the final decade. That back-loaded shape is why starting early beats contributing more later.
A 30-year-old with $0 saved contributes the $7,500 maximum each year until age 65 (35 years), earning an average 7% annual return:
Total contributions: 35 × $7,500 = $262,500
Projected tax-free balance at 65: $1,036,777
Of which tax-free growth: $774,277

chunks.title: Roth IRA Calculator – Project Tax-Free Growth
chunks.text:
Nearly three-quarters of the final million is growth the IRS never touches. Starting at 40 instead of 30 — just ten years later — would cut the outcome roughly in half at the same contribution, which is why the contribution limit matters less than the starting date. From age 50, the $8,600 catch-up limit lets late starters narrow the gap.
# Frequently asked questions
# Can I contribute to a Roth IRA if I already have a 401(k)?
Yes — the accounts are independent and the limits are separate. You can max out a workplace 401(k) and still contribute the full $7,500 (or $8,600 at 50+) to a Roth IRA in the same year, as long as your income is within the Roth phaseout ranges.
# Do I need earned income to contribute?
Yes. Your contribution cannot exceed your earned income for the year — a student with $3,000 of part-time wages can contribute at most $3,000, even though the headline limit is $7,500. Unearned income like dividends or rental income does not qualify.
# What happens if I contribute more than the limit?

chunks.title: Roth IRA Calculator – Project Tax-Free Growth
chunks.text:
The excess is hit with a 6% excise tax every year it stays in the account. Fix it by withdrawing the excess (plus any earnings on it) before the tax filing deadline, or by applying it to the next year’s contribution.
# Can I convert an existing Traditional IRA to a Roth?
Yes, through a Roth conversion — you pay ordinary income tax on the converted pre-tax amount in the conversion year, and everything after grows tax-free. It is most attractive in low-income years, early retirement gaps, or market dips when the balance (and the tax bill) is temporarily smaller.
# Should I pick Roth or Traditional contributions in my workplace 401(k)?
Apply the same logic as the IRA choice: Roth 401(k) contributions suit years when your tax rate is low (early career), while traditional pre-tax contributions suit peak-earning years when the deduction is most valuable. Many savers split between the two to diversify their future tax exposure.
# What should I invest in inside the Roth IRA?

chunks.title: Roth IRA Calculator – Project Tax-Free Growth
chunks.text:
The account is a tax wrapper, not an investment — you still choose the holdings. Because withdrawals are tax-free, assets with the highest expected growth (broad stock index funds, for most savers) benefit most from being sheltered here rather than in a taxable account.
See how contributions change your current tax bill with our Income Tax Calculator , check the take-home impact of retirement deductions in the Paycheck Calculator , make sure housing costs leave room to save with the Mortgage Affordability Calculator , or model the mortgage itself in the Mortgage Loan Calculator .

chunks.title: HELOC Calculator – Payments & Credit Limit Estimator
chunks.text:
Estimate your credit line from home equity, plus draw-period and repayment payments.
# How a HELOC works: draw vs. repayment
A home equity line of credit works like a credit card secured by your house. During the draw period (typically 10 years) you borrow and repay flexibly with interest-only payments. Then the repayment period begins (often 15 years) with amortized principal-and-interest payments.
# How much can you borrow? Understanding LTV
Lenders cap total secured debt at ~80% of appraised value. Formula: (home value × max LTV) − mortgage owed = credit line. On $500,000 with $300,000 owed at 80% LTV: $100,000.
# The variable-rate warning
Almost all HELOCs charge variable rates tied to prime. Ask for the lifetime cap and worst-case payment before signing. If your budget can’t absorb a 2–3 point rise, a fixed home equity loan may be safer.
# How much can I borrow with a HELOC?
Typically up to 80% of appraised value minus mortgage balance — about $100,000 on a $500,000 home owing $300,000.
# What is the interest-only draw period?
Usually the first 10 years: borrow and repay flexibly, paying only interest on drawn balances. Then ~15 years of P&I repayment.

chunks.title: HELOC Calculator – Payments & Credit Limit Estimator
chunks.text:
# Is HELOC interest tax-deductible?
Only if funds buy, build, or substantially improve the securing home, and only if you itemize. Consult a tax advisor.
# HELOC vs. home equity loan?
HELOC: flexible reusable credit, variable rate. Home equity loan: lump sum, fixed rate, payment certainty.
# What if my home value drops?
Lenders can freeze or reduce your line. Borrowing well under your maximum protects against this.
# How to use this calculator
A HELOC has two distinct phases — the draw period and the repayment period — so the calculator needs inputs for both. Fill them in this order:
Home value. Your best estimate of the current appraised value, not the purchase price. A recent comparable sale on your street or a professional appraisal is far more reliable than an automated online estimate.
Current mortgage balance owed. What remains on your first mortgage. The calculator subtracts this from your allowable equity to find your credit line.
Maximum LTV. Lenders typically cap total secured debt at 80% of appraised value. The default 80% is the industry standard; some lenders allow 85–90% at higher rates. The formula is: (home value × max LTV) − mortgage owed = credit line.

chunks.title: HELOC Calculator – Payments & Credit Limit Estimator
chunks.text:
Interest rate. The variable rate you have been quoted, usually expressed as prime plus a margin. Because HELOC rates move with prime, also note the lifetime cap from your disclosure.
Draw period length. Usually 10 years: the window when you can borrow, repay, and re-borrow, typically with interest-only minimum payments.
Repayment period length. Usually 15 years after the draw period ends: borrowing stops and the balance amortizes with principal-and-interest payments.
# Understanding your results
Max credit line. The maximum the lender is likely to extend, from the LTV formula — the headline number. Borrowing well under this maximum protects you if the lender freezes or reduces the line during a downturn.
Draw-period payment (interest-only). The interest-only minimum computed on the full credit line — the cheapest your monthly cost will ever be. Budgeting only this number is the classic HELOC trap.
Repayment payment (P&I). The fully amortized principal-and-interest payment once the draw period ends. This is the number your long-term budget must absorb — it is typically 30–50% higher than the interest-only payment on the same balance.

chunks.title: HELOC Calculator – Payments & Credit Limit Estimator
chunks.text:
Home equity. Your total equity (home value minus mortgage owed) — the raw material the line is drawn from.
Equity remaining after max line. The cushion left untouched if you borrowed the full line. Lenders like to see a buffer here; a thin cushion means any price dip could freeze your line.
A homeowner’s house is worth $500,000 with $300,000 owed on the first mortgage. At 80% maximum LTV the estimated credit line is $100,000 (($500,000 × 0.80) − $300,000). At a variable rate currently 8.50% , with a 10-year draw and 15-year repayment:
Draw-period payment (interest-only on the full line): $708.33/month ($100,000 × 8.50% ÷ 12)
Repayment-period payment (15-year amortization): $984.74/month
Home equity: $200,000 ; equity remaining after max line: $100,000
The lesson: the $708 interest-only payment is temporary by design. Underwrite yourself on the $985 repayment figure — and remember that as a variable-rate product, both numbers rise if prime rises.
# Frequently asked questions
# Should I pay principal during the draw period?

chunks.title: HELOC Calculator – Payments & Credit Limit Estimator
chunks.text:
You are only required to pay interest, but every principal dollar you send during the draw period is a dollar you will not amortize later at a possibly higher rate. Borrowers who treat the draw period as interest-only for the full ten years face the maximum payment shock when repayment begins.
# Can I lock a fixed rate on part of my HELOC?
Many lenders offer a fixed-rate lock option letting you convert a portion of the drawn balance to a fixed rate and fixed payment, similar to a mini home-equity loan inside the line. Ask whether your product includes it and whether each lock carries a fee — it is the cheapest hedge against rising prime.
# Are there annual fees or minimum draw requirements?
Often yes. Common terms include a $50–$75 annual fee, a minimum initial draw ($10,000 is typical), and sometimes a minimum balance to keep the line open. These are disclosed in the account agreement but rarely in the advertised rate — read the fee schedule before comparing offers.
# How quickly can I access HELOC funds?

chunks.title: HELOC Calculator – Payments & Credit Limit Estimator
chunks.text:
From application to funding is typically 2–6 weeks: valuation, underwriting, and a three-day right-of-rescission period on primary residences. After that, draws are usually instant via online transfer or checks — that on-demand access is the product’s main advantage over a lump-sum loan.
# Can I use a HELOC as a down payment on another property?
Lenders allow it, but the second property’s mortgage lender will count the HELOC payment in your debt-to-income ratio, which can torpedo the new approval. It also concentrates leverage on your primary home. Investors do it routinely; first-time buyers should model the combined payments carefully first.
