chunks.title: Mortgage Points Break-Even: Are Discount Points Worth It?
chunks.text:
# Mortgage Points Break-Even: Are Discount Points Worth It?
Mortgage points are worth buying only if you keep the loan past the break-even point: the points cost divided by the monthly saving. On a $400,000 loan, one point costs $4,000, saves $65.40 a month, and breaks even in about 61 months. Keep the loan longer than that and the points profit; sell or refinance sooner and the money is wasted.
At closing, your lender will offer this trade: pay cash now in the form of discount points , and your interest rate drops for the next 30 years. Whether that trade helps you depends on one thing — how long you will actually keep this loan. This guide shows how the mortgage points break-even works, with real numbers, and when buying points makes sense.
# What discount points are
One discount point costs 1% of the loan amount and typically buys a 0.25% reduction in your interest rate. On a $400,000 loan, one point is $4,000 upfront for roughly a quarter-point off the rate. You can usually buy in fractions (half points, quarter points) or stack multiple points, and the rate reduction scales roughly linearly.

chunks.title: Mortgage Points Break-Even: Are Discount Points Worth It?
chunks.text:
Points are not the same as origination fees or lender credits . Origination fees are the lender’s charge for making the loan — they do not lower your rate. Lender credits work the opposite way to points: the lender pays you (as a closing-cost credit) in exchange for a higher rate. All three sit on the same rate-versus-cash tradeoff curve, so always ask your lender to quote all three versions.
# The mortgage points break-even formula (with real numbers)
The whole decision comes down to one division:
Break-even (months) = points cost ÷ monthly payment savings
Worked example — $400,000 loan, 30-year term :
At 6.50% with no points: $2,528.27/month
Buy 1 point ($4,000) → rate drops to ~ 6.25% : $2,462.87/month
Monthly savings: $65.40
Break-even: $4,000 ÷ $65.40 ≈ 61 months (just over 5 years)
Buy 2 points ($8,000) → rate ~ 6.00% : payment $2,398.20, savings $130.07/month , break-even $8,000 ÷ $130.07 ≈ 61.5 months . The break-even barely moves, because each point buys a similar rate cut, so the payback period stays roughly constant. What changes is the total profit after break-even: two points earn double the monthly savings for the rest of the loan.

chunks.title: Mortgage Points Break-Even: Are Discount Points Worth It?
chunks.text:
Run the same division on your own figures in the Mortgage Calculator — get the payment with and without points, then divide the points cost by the difference.
The rule is simple: if you’ll keep the loan past the break-even month, points win; if you’ll sell or refinance before it, points lose. Every payment after month 61 is pure profit on the 1-point deal — about $785 a year, every year, for up to 25 more years.
# When buying points makes sense
You’re staying long-term. This is the big one. Buying points on a “forever home” you plan to keep 10+ years is usually a clear win. On a starter home you’ll sell in 4 years, it’s a guaranteed loss.
You have the cash without strain. Points compete with your down payment, emergency fund, and moving costs for the same dollars. Never buy points with money that leaves you cash-poor at closing.
You’re already at a good rate. Points stack on top of whatever rate you’ve negotiated — shop the base rate first, then price points. A lender quoting a high rate with “cheap” points is just moving money between pockets.

chunks.title: Mortgage Points Break-Even: Are Discount Points Worth It?
chunks.text:
You itemize deductions. Points paid on a purchase mortgage are generally deductible as mortgage interest in the year paid (consult a tax advisor for your situation), which shortens the effective break-even.
# When points are a trap
You might refinance soon. Refinancing replaces the loan — and wipes out any unrecovered points. If there’s a realistic chance rates fall within your break-even window, skip the points; you can buy them (or not) on the refinance instead. The Refinance Calculator helps you check whether a refinance is likely to pay off soon.
Your time horizon is short. Job relocations, growing families, and upsizing plans kill point investments early. Be honest about how long you’ll stay.
The break-even exceeds ~7 years. Lenders sometimes price points poorly (a point buying only 0.125% off). If the math needs a decade to pay back, the points are overpriced — negotiate the base rate instead.
Cash is tight. Every dollar in points is a dollar not in your emergency fund. The return on points is slow and certain; the return on a cash cushion is surviving the surprise roof repair.
# Points vs. a bigger down payment

chunks.title: Mortgage Points Break-Even: Are Discount Points Worth It?
chunks.text:
A common dilemma: $4,000 toward points, or $4,000 more down? The down payment reduces your loan balance permanently — lowering the payment and the total interest and possibly your PMI. Points only lower the rate. As a rule of thumb, if you’re below 20% down, the extra down payment usually wins (PMI savings amplify it) — the PMI Calculator shows what that insurance is costing you. If you’re already at 20%+, compare the two directly: work out the payment both ways and pick the lower one. There is no universal winner — it’s arithmetic, not philosophy.
# How to negotiate points like a pro
Points are priced on a rate sheet the lender doesn’t volunteer — so ask directly: “What is my rate with zero points, and what does each quarter-point of rate reduction cost?” Get this in writing on the Loan Estimate, then:
Shop the base rate first. Negotiate the zero-point rate across 3+ lenders before discussing points. A lender offering “cheap points” on an inflated base rate is just moving your money between line items.

chunks.title: Mortgage Points Break-Even: Are Discount Points Worth It?
chunks.text:
Ask for the full menu. Lenders can quote any combination — 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 points. The per-point price often improves as you buy more (the second point sometimes buys a bigger cut than the first), so price each increment separately.
Compare against lender credits. Ask what credit they’d give you for taking a rate 0.25% higher . Sometimes the credit for going up exceeds the cost of going down — an asymmetry you can use if you’re cash-constrained at closing.
Time it. You generally lock your rate-and-points combination together. If you lock early and rates fall before closing, ask about a float-down option rather than mourning the points.
The same math applies on refinances — but the horizon is what matters. Points on a refinance you’ll keep for 15 years are usually a better deal than points on a purchase you might exit in 7, because refinance borrowers have already shown how long they stay.
# Finding points on your Loan Estimate

chunks.title: Mortgage Points Break-Even: Are Discount Points Worth It?
chunks.text:
Lenders must disclose points on the standardized Loan Estimate form — page 2, section A (“Origination Charges”). Discount points appear as a named line item (e.g., “Discount points — 1.000%”), separate from origination fees. When comparing lenders, line up their Loan Estimates side by side and compare total section-A costs at the same rate — a lender quoting a lower rate with two points isn’t cheaper than a lender quoting a higher rate with zero points until you run the break-even on the difference. The Loan Estimate makes this comparison mechanical: same rate, lowest total cost wins; different rates, break-even math decides.
1 point = 1% of the loan upfront ≈ 0.25% off your rate.
Break-even = points cost ÷ monthly savings. On $400K, 1 point breaks even in ~61 months.
Keep the loan past break-even and points profit; sell or refinance before it and they lose.
Never buy points with emergency-fund money, and never buy them if a refinance is likely soon.
Below 20% down, extra down payment usually beats points.
# Frequently asked questions
# How much does one mortgage point lower my rate?

chunks.title: Mortgage Points Break-Even: Are Discount Points Worth It?
chunks.text:
Typically about 0.25%, though it varies by lender and market — always ask for the exact rate with and without points. Some lenders offer worse deals (0.125% per point); those points are usually overpriced.
# Are discount points tax-deductible?
Points paid on a loan to buy your primary residence are generally deductible as mortgage interest in the year you pay them, provided you meet IRS conditions. Points on a refinance are usually deducted over the life of the loan instead. Tax law changes, so confirm with a tax advisor.
# Can I buy fractional points?
Yes — most lenders sell points in eighths or quarters (0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75). There’s nothing special about whole numbers; price the exact break-even for whatever fraction is offered.
# Do points make sense on an ARM?
Rarely. The break-even math assumes you keep the rate for decades, but an ARM’s rate resets in 5–10 years. Unless the point discount is unusually generous, skip points on adjustable-rate loans.
# What’s the difference between discount points and origination fees?

chunks.title: Mortgage Points Break-Even: Are Discount Points Worth It?
chunks.text:
Discount points buy a lower rate; origination fees are simply the lender’s charge for processing the loan and buy nothing. Both appear on your Loan Estimate — compare lenders on total cost, not on any single line.
# Can I roll points into the loan instead of paying cash?
Some lenders allow it, but financing the points means paying interest on them for 30 years, which lengthens the break-even considerably. Paying cash at closing is almost always the better deal if you buy points at all.

chunks.title: 15-Year vs 30-Year Mortgage: Which Term Wins?
chunks.text:
# 15-Year vs 30-Year Mortgage: Which Term Wins?
On a $400,000 loan at 6.50% , a 15-year mortgage costs $956.16 more per month than a 30-year mortgage but saves $282,981 in lifetime interest. The 15-year term builds equity far faster; the 30-year term keeps the required payment low and your options open. The right choice depends less on the interest total than on how stable your cash flow is.
That term checkbox shapes more than the payment. It sets when you own your home outright, how much risk you carry if income drops, and how quickly your balance falls. Both terms can be the right answer — for completely different households. The numbers below show why.
# 15-year vs 30-year mortgage: the tradeoff in real numbers
Take a $400,000 loan at 6.50% — the same scenario, two different terms:
30-year: $2,528.27/month — total interest $510,178
15-year: $3,484.43/month — total interest $227,197
Difference: $956.16 more per month buys $282,981 less in lifetime interest

chunks.title: 15-Year vs 30-Year Mortgage: Which Term Wins?
chunks.text:
The 15-year payment is about 38% higher, but the interest bill drops by more than half. Two forces combine to produce that gap: you pay for half as many years, and 15-year rates are typically 0.5–0.75% lower than 30-year rates to begin with (the example above holds the rate equal to isolate the term effect — in practice the 15-year advantage is even larger).
# Why the 15-year builds wealth so much faster
It’s not just the shorter clock — it’s the amortization curve. On a 30-year loan, your first payment of $2,528 sends roughly $2,167 to interest and only $361 to principal: 86% interest. On the 15-year loan, the first $3,484 payment sends $2,167 to interest and $1,317 to principal. Same interest, triple the equity.
After five years, the 30-year borrower still owes about 92% of the original balance; the 15-year borrower owes roughly 76%. That equity gap compounds: the 15-year borrower can sell, refinance, or borrow against the home from a position of strength years earlier. If your plan involves moving up, tapping equity, or retiring without a mortgage payment, the 15-year term front-loads all of it.
# The case for the 30-year: flexibility and liquidity

chunks.title: 15-Year vs 30-Year Mortgage: Which Term Wins?
chunks.text:
The 30-year’s higher interest bill buys something real: optionality . The lower required payment is a floor, not a ceiling — nothing stops a 30-year borrower from paying extra. Consider what the $956 monthly difference can do:
Emergency resilience: if income drops, you can fall back to the lower required payment. A 15-year borrower has no such escape hatch — the higher payment is mandatory every month.
Investing the difference: $956.16 invested monthly at a 7% average annual return grows to roughly $1,166,487 over 30 years (about $344,218 of it contributions). That dwarfs the $282,981 of interest saved by the 15-year term — if you actually invest it, if returns cooperate, and after taxes and risk. Those are three big ifs, which is why this debate never ends.
Inflation hedge: a fixed 30-year payment gets cheaper in real terms every year. In year 25, that $2,528 buys far less than it does today — you’re repaying with discounted dollars.
The honest version of the 30-year strategy: take the lower payment, then actually prepay or invest the difference. The dishonest version — spending it — is how the 30-year becomes the most expensive choice.

chunks.title: 15-Year vs 30-Year Mortgage: Which Term Wins?
chunks.text:
# Who should pick a 15-year vs a 30-year mortgage?
Lean 15-year if: the higher payment fits comfortably (ideally under 28% of gross income), you have a full emergency fund covering 3–6 months of expenses, you’re buying a long-term home, and you’re within 15–20 years of retirement — entering retirement without a mortgage payment is one of the highest-value financial moves available.
Lean 30-year if: you’re stretching to buy in an expensive market, your income is variable, you’re early in your career with rising earnings ahead, or you’d rather keep cash liquid for investing, a business, or upcoming expenses. Then automate extra principal payments so the flexibility doesn’t become procrastination.
Consider the middle path: a 20-year term splits the difference — meaningfully less interest than 30, meaningfully more breathing room than 15. And any 30-year borrower can simulate a shorter term with systematic extra payments; our Mortgage Extra Payment Calculator shows exactly what each extra dollar buys.
# What about refinancing into a 15-year later?

chunks.title: 15-Year vs 30-Year Mortgage: Which Term Wins?
chunks.text:
It’s a legitimate strategy: buy with a 30-year, then refinance into a 15-year once your income grows or rates fall. But price it honestly — you’ll pay closing costs a second time (typically 2–5% of the loan), and the years you spent on the 30-year schedule were mostly interest. Refinancing from year 5 of a 30-year into a fresh 15-year still beats staying the course, but starting with the 15-year would have beaten both. Run the comparison in our Mortgage Refinance Calculator before you assume the later switch is free.
# Three borrower profiles: who actually picks what
Profile 1 — Maya, 29, first-time buyer, $95K income, expensive metro. The 15-year payment would consume 44% of her gross income — she can’t qualify, and shouldn’t try. She takes the 30-year, automates a $200/month extra principal payment, and plans to refinance into a 15-year once her income grows. Verdict: 30-year, used wisely.

chunks.title: 15-Year vs 30-Year Mortgage: Which Term Wins?
chunks.text:
Profile 2 — David and Priya, 45, $210K combined income, buying their “forever” home. The 15-year payment is 24% of gross — comfortable. They’ll be mortgage-free at 60, right as they want to ramp down work. The $282,981 in saved interest is worth more to them than market speculation. Verdict: 15-year.
Profile 3 — Sam, 38, freelancer with lumpy $140K income. Some months he earns $20K, some months $4K. The 15-year’s mandatory higher payment would be dangerous in lean months. He takes the 30-year and prepays aggressively in flush months — capturing most of the 15-year’s savings with none of its rigidity. Verdict: 30-year + voluntary prepayment.
Notice the pattern: the decision follows cash-flow stability more than income level. Stable, ample cash flow → 15-year. Variable or stretched cash flow → 30-year with discipline.
# The 20-year compromise

chunks.title: 15-Year vs 30-Year Mortgage: Which Term Wins?
chunks.text:
Can’t decide? The 20-year term is the underrated middle path. On our $400,000 at 6.50% example, a 20-year payment runs about $2,982/month — roughly $454 more than the 30-year but $502 less than the 15-year — with total interest around $315,700, saving nearly $194,500 versus the 30-year. You capture most of the 15-year’s interest savings while keeping the payment meaningfully below the 15-year’s level. Fewer lenders advertise 20-year products, so ask explicitly — and if it’s unavailable, remember that a 30-year loan with a $454/month extra principal payment replicates it almost exactly, with the added freedom to stop the extras whenever you need to.
On $400,000 at 6.50%, the 15-year costs $956/month more but saves $282,981 in interest.
The 15-year builds equity dramatically faster — ~24% paid down in 5 years vs ~8% on the 30-year.
The 30-year’s edge is flexibility: lower mandatory payment, liquidity, and the option to invest the difference.
“Invest the difference” only wins if you actually invest it — automating beats intending.
A 20-year term or systematic extra payments on a 30-year can split the difference.
# Frequently asked questions

chunks.title: 15-Year vs 30-Year Mortgage: Which Term Wins?
chunks.text:
# Is a 15-year mortgage always better than a 30-year?
No — it’s cheaper in interest but demands a much higher monthly payment with no flexibility. For buyers stretching to afford a home or with variable income, the 30-year’s lower mandatory payment is the safer foundation, especially if you prepay voluntarily.
# Do 15-year mortgages have lower interest rates?
Usually, yes — typically 0.5 to 0.75 percentage points below 30-year rates, because the lender’s money is at risk for half as long. That rate advantage is on top of the term savings shown above.
# Can I pay a 30-year mortgage like a 15-year?
Yes. Paying the 15-year payment amount on a 30-year loan retires it in about 15 years (at the same rate). The difference: you can stop the extra payments any time, while the 15-year borrower cannot. Use an extra-payment calculator to find your exact payoff date.
# Which term is better if I might move in 7 years?
Usually the 15-year — or a 30-year with aggressive prepayments. After 7 years the 15-year borrower has built roughly twice the equity, which matters enormously when you sell and need a down payment for the next home.
# Does the term affect my approval amount?

chunks.title: 15-Year vs 30-Year Mortgage: Which Term Wins?
chunks.text:
Yes. Lenders qualify you on the actual payment, so the higher 15-year payment means you qualify for a smaller loan at the same income. If you’re already near your DTI limits, the 30-year may be the only way to buy the home you want.
# Should I refinance from a 30-year to a 15-year?
It can be a wealth-building move if the higher payment fits and you plan to stay long enough to recover closing costs. But compare it against simply making extra payments on your current loan — refinancing restarts the clock and costs 2–5% of the balance.
Model both terms side by side in the Mortgage Loan Calculator , see the payment-by-payment difference in the Mortgage Amortization Schedule Calculator , simulate prepaying a 30-year like a 15-year in the Mortgage Extra Payment Calculator , or price the refinance switch in the Mortgage Refinance Calculator .

chunks.title: The 28/36 Rule: How Lenders Size Up Your Mortgage
chunks.text:
When a lender decides how much house you can afford, they don’t start with the listing price. They start with two percentages: 28 and 36 . Known as the 28/36 rule, these two numbers are the lending industry’s classic shorthand for the debt-to-income (DTI) limits that separate an approvable mortgage from a declined one. Whether you’re buying your first home or your fifth, understanding these ratios — and where you stand against them — is the single most useful thing you can do before you talk to a lender.
# What the two numbers mean
The rule has two halves, called the front-end ratio and the back-end ratio .
The front-end ratio caps your housing costs at 28% of your gross monthly income. Housing costs means the full PITI payment: principal and interest, property taxes, homeowner’s insurance, plus any HOA dues and mortgage insurance. Not just the loan payment — everything it costs to keep the roof.
The back-end ratio caps all your monthly debt payments at 36% of gross monthly income. That includes the housing payment plus car loans, student loans, credit-card minimums, personal loans, and child support. Lenders count minimum required debt payments — not rent, utilities, or groceries.

chunks.title: The 28/36 Rule: How Lenders Size Up Your Mortgage
chunks.text:
Both ratios use gross income (pre-tax), not take-home pay. That flatters affordability slightly, since taxes never appear in the ratio — which is why you should always sanity-check the lender’s ceiling against your actual take-home pay before falling in love with a listing.
# Worked example: $120,000 household income
Take a household earning $120,000 per year , or $10,000 per month, with $800 per month in existing debt payments (a car loan and student loans).
Front-end cap: $10,000 × 28% = $2,800/month maximum for all housing costs.
Back-end cap: $10,000 × 36% = $3,600/month maximum for housing plus all debts.
Housing budget after debts: $3,600 − $800 = $2,800/month for housing.
In this case both ratios agree: the household can spend up to $2,800 a month on housing. If the same household had $1,500 in monthly debts instead, the back-end ratio would bind first: $3,600 − $1,500 = $2,100, and the housing budget would shrink to $2,100 even though the front-end ratio still allows $2,800. The lower of the two results always wins — that is the whole point of having two ratios.
# How lenders actually use it (and where they bend)

chunks.title: The 28/36 Rule: How Lenders Size Up Your Mortgage
chunks.text:
The 28/36 rule is the textbook version. In practice, different loan programs draw the lines in slightly different places:
Conventional loans (Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac) commonly allow back-end ratios up to 43–45% with strong compensating factors — a high credit score, large cash reserves, or a big down payment.
FHA loans are more generous still, often approving back-end ratios into the 50s for borrowers with solid credit and reserves.
VA loans don’t publish a hard DTI cap at all, though lenders still scrutinize the borrower’s residual income.
Our Mortgage Affordability Calculator uses the conservative 36% back-end figure as its baseline, so treat its ceiling as a safe starting point rather than the absolute maximum a lender might offer. Being approved at 50% DTI and being comfortable at 50% DTI are very different things.
# How to improve your ratios before you apply
You have three levers, and they work in this order of impact:

chunks.title: The 28/36 Rule: How Lenders Size Up Your Mortgage
chunks.text:
1. Pay down monthly debts. Eliminating a $400 car payment doesn’t just save $400 — at a 36% back-end ratio, it frees up $400 of monthly housing budget, which supports roughly $63,000 more in loan amount at 6.5% over 30 years. Small debts with big minimums are the highest-return payoff targets before a mortgage application.
2. Increase your down payment. A larger down payment shrinks the loan, which shrinks the payment, which improves the front-end ratio directly. It also helps you dodge private mortgage insurance, which counts inside the housing payment.
3. Raise your income — carefully. Lenders count stable, documented income: salary, steady bonuses, two-year histories of freelance or side income. A brand-new second job or a one-time windfall generally doesn’t count.
What doesn’t help: closing old credit cards (it can hurt your score), or shifting debt between cards. Lenders look at minimum payments and balances, not how cleverly the debt is arranged.
# The 28/36 rule vs. real life

chunks.title: The 28/36 Rule: How Lenders Size Up Your Mortgage
chunks.text:
The ratios are guardrails, not a budget. A household at exactly 36% back-end DTI with high childcare costs, expensive health insurance, or lumpy freelance income will feel far more stretched than the ratio suggests — because none of those appear in the lender’s math. Financial planners often advise first-time buyers, single-income households, and anyone without a deep emergency fund to target housing under 25–28% of gross (or roughly 35% of take-home) rather than stretching to the maximum approval. The lender’s job is to measure default risk; your job is to measure your life.
# What if you’re over the limits?
Failing the 28/36 test with a lender doesn’t mean homeownership is off the table — it means the current combination of price, down payment, and debt doesn’t work. You have five moves, roughly in order of effectiveness:
Buy less house. The fastest fix. Every $10,000 off the price cuts roughly $64/month from a 6.5%/30-year payment — and it improves both ratios at once.
Grow the down payment. Dropping from a $400,000 loan to $360,000 (10% down instead of 5% on the same price) cuts the payment by about $253/month and may eliminate PMI, which helps the front-end ratio twice.

chunks.title: The 28/36 Rule: How Lenders Size Up Your Mortgage
chunks.text:
Kill a monthly debt entirely. Lenders count minimum payments, so eliminating one $300/month obligation frees $300 of back-end room — often more impactful than the same dollars added to a down payment.
Add a co-borrower. A partner’s income counts (along with their debts and credit). Run the combined ratios before assuming it helps — a partner with heavy student loans can hurt more than their income helps.
Wait and repair. Six months of aggressive debt payoff can move both ratios dramatically. A mortgage is a 30-year commitment; a 6-month delay to qualify cleanly is cheap insurance.
What not to do: stretch into an interest-only or adjustable product just to pass the ratios. Qualifying on a teaser payment you’ll never actually afford is how the 2008 crisis happened — the ratios exist to protect you, not just the lender.
# DTI bands: where do you stand?
Not all DTI ratios are equal. Here’s how lenders generally read your back-end ratio:
Under 28%: excellent — you’ll qualify for the best programs and have the most negotiating leverage.
28–36%: the comfort zone — standard approvals with good pricing across conventional, FHA, and VA.

chunks.title: The 28/36 Rule: How Lenders Size Up Your Mortgage
chunks.text:
36–43%: workable — conventional approval is common with compensating factors; expect more documentation.
43–50%: stretched — FHA territory or conventional with strong reserves and credit; pricing suffers.
Over 50%: difficult — limited to specialized programs; most planners would call this overextended regardless of approval.
Compute yours now: add every monthly minimum debt payment (including the proposed housing payment), divide by gross monthly income. If you’re above 43%, treat debt reduction as step one of your homebuying plan — not an afterthought.
Spend no more than 28% of gross monthly income on total housing costs (front-end ratio).
Keep all monthly debt payments, including housing, under 36% of gross income (back-end ratio).
The lower of the two calculations sets your real budget.
Conventional, FHA, and VA programs allow higher ratios — but approval is not the same as affordability.
Paying off high-minimum debts before applying is the fastest way to raise your ceiling.
# Frequently asked questions
# Is the 28/36 rule a law?

chunks.title: The 28/36 Rule: How Lenders Size Up Your Mortgage
chunks.text:
No — it’s an industry guideline, not a statute. Individual lenders and loan programs set their own DTI caps, and many approve borrowers well above 36% back-end with compensating strengths. But 28/36 remains the benchmark underwriters are trained on, so it’s the right planning target.
# Do lenders use gross or net income for DTI?
Gross — pre-tax income. This makes the ratios slightly more generous than they feel in take-home terms, which is why you should always cross-check the resulting payment against your actual budget.
# What counts as a “debt” in the back-end ratio?
Minimum payments on installment and revolving debt: car loans, student loans, credit-card minimums, personal loans, child support, and alimony. Rent, utilities, insurance premiums, and groceries don’t count — though your budget must cover them.
# Can I get a mortgage above a 43% back-end ratio?
Sometimes. FHA loans and some conventional programs approve higher ratios with strong compensating factors like excellent credit, large reserves, or residual income. Expect more documentation and scrutiny.
# Does the 28/36 rule apply to refinances too?

chunks.title: The 28/36 Rule: How Lenders Size Up Your Mortgage
chunks.text:
Yes — lenders re-verify DTI on every mortgage application, including refinances. A refinance that looked easy at origination can get harder if your debts grew or your income fell since you bought.
# How is DTI different from my credit score?
DTI measures cash-flow capacity (can you afford the payment?); the credit score measures repayment history (do you pay on time?). Lenders need both: a great score won’t fix a 60% DTI, and a low DTI won’t fix a 580 score.

South Dakota’s typical home value is about $321,600 as of August 2026 (Zillow ZHVI), with Sioux Falls and Rapid City leading growth. # South Dakota mortgage facts

# South Dakota first-time buyer programs

chunks.title: South Dakota Mortgage Calculator – Payment Estimator
chunks.text:
SDHDA First-Time Homebuyer Program — Low-interest, fixed-rate 30-year mortgages for eligible buyers who haven’t owned in 3 years and meet income and purchase price limits; work with SDHDA participating lenders. Official site
SDHDA Fixed Rate Plus — 3% to 5% of the loan amount for down payment/closing costs as a 0%-interest second mortgage with no required payments (repaid at sale/refi/payoff); paired with an SDHDA first mortgage at a slightly higher rate. Official site
# How to use this calculator
The calculator comes pre-filled with South Dakota’s $321,574 median home price, the state’s 1.00% effective property tax rate, and the $1,756/year average insurance premium. Set your down payment — with SDHDA’s Fixed Rate Plus you can get 3–5% of the loan covered, but remember that option carries a slightly higher first-mortgage rate, so model both scenarios. The 2026 conforming limit is $832,750 statewide; jumbo territory is rarely relevant here. Adjust the rate to your actual lender quote (2026 rates are running in the mid-6s) and note that SDHDA programs have their own county income and purchase price caps.
# Worked example: a median South Dakota home

chunks.title: South Dakota Mortgage Calculator – Payment Estimator
chunks.text:
Take a median-priced South Dakota home at $321,574. With 20% down ($64,314.80), the loan amount is $257,259.20. At 7.40% (Freddie Mac PMMS, week ending October 15, 2026) on a 30-year fixed term, principal and interest come to $1,781.21/month . Add property tax of about $267.98/month (1.0% of $321,574, divided by 12) and insurance of about $146.33/month ($1,756 a year), for a total estimated payment of $2,195.52/month . Over 30 years, total interest would be about $383,976.66. Your rate, down payment, and county tax bill will move these numbers — use the calculator above with your own figures.
# What is the 2026 conforming loan limit in South Dakota?
The 2026 FHFA baseline of $832,750 applies in every South Dakota county — there are no high-cost counties in the state. Loans above $832,750 are jumbo.
# How does Fixed Rate Plus assistance work?

chunks.title: South Dakota Mortgage Calculator – Payment Estimator
chunks.text:
SDHDA’s Fixed Rate Plus provides 3% to 5% of the loan amount for down payment and closing costs as a 0%-interest second mortgage with no required payments — it is repaid when you sell, refinance, or pay off the first mortgage. The trade-off is a slightly higher interest rate on the first mortgage, and you must meet income limits and complete homebuyer education.
# Does South Dakota offer a Mortgage Credit Certificate?
Yes — SD Housing offers an MCC, a federal income tax credit based on the mortgage interest you pay each year, which can be combined with other assistance programs. It is claimed annually on your tax return for as long as you live in the home.
# How do taxes work with no state income tax?
South Dakota has no state income tax, and the median effective property tax rate is an even 1.00% (Tax Foundation 2026) — roughly $3,216 a year on the $321,574 statewide median home value. Property tax is the main local revenue source, so rates vary by county and school district.
# What is the Governor’s House program?

chunks.title: South Dakota Mortgage Calculator – Payment Estimator
chunks.text: SDHDA’s Governor’s House program sells affordable, energy-efficient homes — built through a prison rehabilitation program — at reduced prices to income-qualified buyers. It is a separate path from the standard First-Time Homebuyer mortgage program for buyers open to new construction on a budget.

chunks.title: New Mexico Mortgage Calculator – Payment Estimator

Yes — most New Mexico purchases use a deed of trust rather than a mortgage, which allows non-judicial foreclosure if you fall seriously behind. The practical takeaway: keep payments current and communicate with your servicer early if you hit trouble, since the foreclosure timeline can move faster than in judicial-foreclosure states.
